readerTitle: Spanx started with $5,000 and never took investor money
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Spanx, 창업자 Sara Blakely, 2021년 Blackstone 투자) + 가상 적용 (치과용 예약 소프트웨어)
insight: 투자를 받을지는 '받을 수 있나'가 아니라 '고객의 돈으로 성장 비용을 댈 수 있나'와 '속도가 승패를 가르나'로 판단한다.
misconception: 제대로 크려면 결국 외부 투자가 필요하다. 투자를 안 받는 건 야망이 작다는 뜻이다.

sources.text: Forbes (2012), Sara Blakely 억만장자 선정 기사 및 커버 스토리 ($5,000 창업 자금, 외부 투자 없음, 100% 지분)
Blackstone 보도자료 (2021년 10월), Spanx 지분 과반 인수 및 기업가치 약 $12억
Spanx 공식 회사 소개 'Our Story' (창업 연도, Neiman Marcus, Oprah)
NPR 'How I Built This' Sara Blakely 인터뷰 (공장 섭외, 특허, Neiman Marcus 화장실 시연 일화)

factChecks.note: 창업 자금 $5,000(개인 저축)과 2000년 출시는 Forbes와 Spanx 공식 자료로 다시 확인하세요.
Neiman Marcus 바이어 앞에서 화장실에서 직접 시연했다는 이야기는 Blakely 본인이 여러 인터뷰에서 한 말입니다. 카드에는 'by her own account'로 적었습니다.
2000년 Oprah의 'Favorite Things' 선정은 Spanx 공식 자료로 확인하세요.
Forbes 2012년 '최연소 자수성가 여성 억만장자' 선정, 2021년 Blackstone 거래 전까지 외부 투자 없이 100% 지분 보유 여부를 확인하세요.
Blackstone 거래 기업가치 약 $12억, Blakely가 상당 지분을 계속 보유했다는 점은 2021년 보도자료로 확인하세요. 정확한 잔여 지분율은 공개 자료마다 달라 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
초기에 팩스기 영업 일을 계속하며 창업을 준비했다는 점과 특허 출원서 상당 부분을 직접 썼다는 점은 인터뷰 기반입니다. 세부(변리사 비용 등)는 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
8번 카드의 소프트웨어 사례는 가상이며 수치(월 5% 성장, 지분 25%)는 설명용입니다.

cards.title: Spanx started with $5,000 and never took investor money
body: In 2000, Sara Blakely launched Spanx, a line of shapewear, using about $5,000 of her own savings. She was selling fax machines at the time.
She raised no outside money. In 2012, Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire. She still owned the whole company.

image.label: A small piggy bank next to a tall stack of shapewear boxes
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 돼지 저금통 하나 옆에 포장 상자가 높이 쌓여 있고, 상자 위로 성장 곡선 화살표. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Orders are coming. Do you raise money?
body: You've built a new kind of undergarment on your savings. A factory makes it for you. A major department store has started stocking it, and a famous TV host has praised it.
Demand could take off. You have almost no money and no team. What do you do?

options.text: Raise money from investors to fund inventory, staff and an ad campaign
options.feedback: You could grow faster and hire help sooner. You'd give up part of the company and some say over its future.

options.text: Keep funding growth from sales and free publicity
options.feedback: You keep full ownership and control. Growth is limited by how fast customers pay you, and you carry the risk alone.

options.text: License the idea to a big hosiery brand for a royalty
options.feedback: Less risk and work for you, and fast reach. But someone else owns the brand and most of the upside.

choice.afterReveal: Blakely chose B. She grew Spanx on its own sales and kept 100% of it for about two decades.

cards.title: She sold first and spent later.
body: Blakely wrote much of her own patent application. Many hosiery mills turned her down before one in North Carolina agreed to make her product.
She cold-called Neiman Marcus and, by her own account, showed the buyer the product in a store restroom. The store took it. Soon after, Oprah Winfrey named Spanx one of her favorite things.
Instead of paying for ads, Blakely promoted it herself, in stores and in the press. Each wave of orders paid for the next.

cards.title: Customer-funded growth
body: **Customer-funded growth**, often called bootstrapping, means paying for expansion with money from sales instead of money from investors.
The real question is not whether investors would say yes. It's whether your customers' payments can cover what growth costs, fast enough to keep up with demand.
If they can, outside money buys you speed. You pay for that speed with **ownership**.

image.label: Loop: sale, cash, more stock, more sales
image.brief: 순환 화살표 인포그래픽. "Sale" → "Cash" → "More stock" → "More sales"가 원을 그리며 이어지고, 원 바깥에 점선으로 "Investor money" 화살표가 들어오려다 멈춘 모습.

cards.title: Why the loop worked for Spanx.
body: Several features of the business let sales pay for growth:
list: **Outsourced making:** an existing mill produced it, so no factory to build
**Retail orders:** stores ordered stock, which showed demand before big bets
**Free attention:** press and word of mouth replaced paid ads
**A small, light product:** cheap to store and ship
cards.callout: Each piece kept the cost of growing below what sales brought in.

cards.title: Owning it meant choosing when to sell.
body: In 2021, the investment firm Blackstone bought a majority stake in Spanx at a value of about **$1.2 billion**. Blakely kept a significant share.
Because she had never sold shares, she decided when to bring in investors, and on what terms.

cards.title: Bootstrapping is a fit, not a virtue.
body: Spanx worked because growth was cheap and sales came early. Many businesses need large sums before the first sale, like a drug, a factory or a complex product.
Bootstrapping is also slower. If rivals with money can grab the market first, patience can cost you the market.
And we hear about the winners. Many self-funded founders stayed small or ran out of savings.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your booking software for dental clinics is profitable. Revenue grows about 5% a month from customer payments alone.
A venture fund offers money to triple your sales team, in exchange for 25% of the company. Two funded rivals are chasing the same clinics. What's your move?

options.text: Take it. More money always means more growth
options.feedback: You'd gain speed, but you'd give up a quarter of a business that already funds itself, without knowing whether speed decides the winner.

options.text: Decline. Investors always cost you control
options.feedback: You keep ownership, and your growth is real. But if clinics rarely switch once they pick a tool, losing the race to rivals could cap your future.

options.text: First check whether clinics lock in to the first tool they choose. Raise only if speed decides who wins
options.feedback: This ties the money to a real need. If early wins stick, raising buys the market. If not, your own revenue can fund the climb.

cards.title: Raise money to buy speed, only when speed is what you lack.
body: If customers can pay for your growth, every share you keep is worth more later.
**Try it today:** write down what your next stage of growth costs, and how many months of sales would pay for it. Then ask: would waiting that long cost me the market?
